usage: Plain noun covering both the rocky ravine and the cold stream inside it
물 attached; the icy water you actually dip your feet in
에서 marks where the activity happens, not 에
시원하다 is the habitual summer adjective for 계곡
examples: 여름엔 계곡이 제일 시원해요.
In summer the valley is the coolest.
Simple opinion; 제일 = most, an easy superlative
계곡에 발 담그니까 너무 시원하다.
Dipping my feet in the stream feels so refreshing.
발(을) 담그다 = dip feet in, the set collocation; 담그니까 = 'now that I dip'
주말에 가족이랑 계곡으로 물놀이 가기로 했어요.
We decided to go play in the water at a valley with family this weekend.
으로 marks the destination you head toward; 물놀이 = water play
nuance: 계곡 (溪谷, 'mountain-stream + valley') names both the V-shaped rocky ravine and, in everyday talk, the cold stream running through it — so 'I'm at the 계곡' usually means standing in the water. The dividing line vs 강 is size and feel: a 강 is a wide, slow river you cross by bridge, while a 계곡 is the narrow, boulder-strewn mountain version with fast cold water. Register is fully neutral and casual; everyone from kids to grandparents says it, and from June to August it's THE budget getaway word, glued to 시원하다 (refreshing) and 물놀이 (water play). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't picture a soft green 'valley' (that scenic basin is closer to 골짜기 in literary use), and don't say 계곡에서 수영하다 expecting a pool — you 물놀이 or 발 담그다, since real 계곡 water is shallow, rocky and freezing.

mistakes: Saying 강 when you mean the mountain stream: 강 is a broad river (한강), but the cold rocky ravine you wade in is 계곡 — using 강 makes Koreans picture a totally different, bigger place.
Spelling it 게곡: the vowel is ㅖ (예), so it must be 계곡, never 게곡.
Treating 계곡 like a swimming pool with 수영하다 — Koreans say 물놀이 하다 or 발 담그다, because 계곡 water is shallow and rocky, not for laps.

usage: Neutral noun for any falls, tiny drop to famous tourist one
수(水) added; stresses the falling water, not the cliff
떨어지다 (to fall) is the natural verb for the water dropping
소리 = sound; the most-mentioned appeal of a falls
examples: 저기 폭포 소리 들려요?
Can you hear the waterfall over there?
들리다 = to be audible; simple yes/no question
비가 많이 와서 폭포 물줄기가 엄청 세요.
It rained a lot, so the waterfall's flow is really strong.
물줄기 = jet/stream of water; 세다 = to be powerful
폭포 앞에서 사진 찍으면 진짜 시원해 보여요.
Photos taken in front of a waterfall really look refreshing.
찍으면 = if/when you take (a photo); 보이다 = to look/appear
nuance: 폭포 (瀑布, 'gushing-spread water') is the plain, neutral word for a waterfall of any size — a small drop tucked in a 계곡 or a famous tourist landmark alike — and it habitually travels with 소리 (sound) and 시원하다 (refreshing) when people explain why they like it. Unlike 계곡 (the ravine/stream you walk into) a 폭포 is the vertical fall itself, so the two often appear together: 계곡 따라 올라가면 폭포가 나와요. The near-synonym to know is 폭포수: 폭포 is the structure/place, while 폭포수 isolates the cascading water (the 수 is hanja 水, water). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb — in English a waterfall 'falls' but learners reach for 내리다; Korean specifically uses 떨어지다 (폭포가 떨어지다), and the water is 세다 (strong), never 빠르다 (fast).

mistakes: Misspelling it 포포 or 폭보: the word is 폭포 — first syllable ends in ㄱ batchim, second begins with ㅍ.
Using 내리다 for the falling water (an English 'comes down' transfer) — the natural verb is 폭포가 떨어지다.
Forcing 폭포수 in casual speech: for everyday 'let's go see a waterfall,' plain 폭포 is right; 폭포수 narrowly means the falling water itself.

usage: Natural rock cave; also figurative for a dark cozy hideout
탐험(探險) = adventurous exploring; standard for tourist caves
안 = the interior; 동굴 안은 시원해요
에 + 들어가다 for entering an enclosed space
examples: 동굴 안은 여름에도 시원해요.
Inside the cave it's cool even in summer.
안은 = inside (as topic); caves stay cold year-round
제주도에서 용암 동굴 구경했어요.
I checked out a lava cave in Jeju.
용암 = lava; 구경하다 is the go-to verb for sightseeing a place
동굴이 너무 어두워서 손전등이 꼭 필요해요.
The cave is so dark that a flashlight is essential.
어둡다 → 어두워서 (ㅂ-irregular); 손전등 = flashlight
nuance: 동굴 (洞窟, 'hollow-cavern') is the standard word for a natural cave, including Korea's famous limestone caverns and Jeju's UNESCO lava tubes that headline day trips, and it pairs almost reflexively with 구경하다 (to look around) or 탐험 (exploration). The synonym to separate it from is bare 굴: 굴 can mean 'cave/hole' but in food contexts means 'oyster,' so 굴 구경 is ambiguous while 동굴 구경 is unmistakably the cave. Register is neutral, and there's a warm figurative use — 동굴 같은 방 (a cave-like room) for a dark, snug space, or 동굴에 들어가다 jokingly for hiding away. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'enter the cave' tempts 동굴로 들어가다, but for going INTO an enclosed space you want 동굴에 들어가다; 로 would imply the route/direction you took, not the entering itself.

Saying 동굴로 들어가다 for simply entering: use 동굴에 들어가다 (에), since 로 signals the direction/path rather than the act of going in.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular in 어둡다: 'because it's dark' is 어두워서, not 어둡어서.

usage: Sheer vertical rock face; also figurative for a dead end / crisis
끝 = edge/end; 절벽 끝에 서다 = stand at the edge
위 = top; sea views are described from 절벽 위
에서 marks the source point of the fall
examples: 여기 절벽이 진짜 높아요.
This cliff here is really tall.
높다 = tall/high; the basic adjective for a cliff
위험하니까 절벽 끝에 너무 가까이 가지 마세요.
It's dangerous, so don't go too close to the cliff edge.
가까이 = closely (adverb); -지 마세요 = polite 'please don't'
저 해안 절벽이 사진 명소라서 사람이 많아요.
Those coastal cliffs are a famous photo spot, so it's crowded.
해안 = coast; 명소(名所) = famous/scenic spot
nuance: 절벽 (絶壁, literally 'cut-off wall') is a sheer, vertical cliff or rock face — the 絶 ('to sever') captures how the ground just drops away, common along Korea's coastlines and hiking ridges where signs warn you to stay back. The contrast learners blur is 절벽 vs 언덕: an 언덕 is a gentle, walkable hill, whereas a 절벽 is a vertical drop you could fall off, so they are opposites in steepness, not synonyms. Register is neutral, but 절벽 carries a vivid figurative life — 절벽 끝에 몰리다 (driven to the cliff's edge) means pushed to the brink, and 재정 절벽 is the 'fiscal cliff.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle of falling: you fall 절벽에서 떨어지다 (에서, the source) — using 에 there would wrongly point to a destination, and don't confuse the scenic 해안 절벽 with a soft 'bluff,' which Korean would not call 절벽.

mistakes: Calling a gentle slope a 절벽: an 언덕 is a small hill you walk up, while 절벽 is a vertical drop — mixing them misstates how dangerous the place is.
Spelling it 절뼉 or 절벅: the correct form is 절벽 with ㄹ batchim on the first syllable.
Saying 절벽에 떨어지다 for falling off: use 절벽에서 떨어지다 (에서 = from the cliff), since 에 would suggest landing onto it.

usage: Coastal mud exposed at low tide; a west-coast specialty
체험(體驗) = hands-on experience; a popular family activity
dig for clams in the mudflat
캐다 = to dig up; the classic mudflat activity
드러나다 = to be revealed, as the tide goes out
examples: 여기가 그 유명한 갯벌이에요.
This is that famous mudflat.
Simple identification; 이에요 = polite 'it is'
썰물 때 갯벌이 쫙 드러나요.
At low tide the mudflat gets fully exposed.
썰물 = ebb/low tide; 쫙 = mimetic for spreading wide open
갯벌은 미끄러우니까 꼭 장화 신고 가세요.
Mudflats are slippery, so be sure to wear rubber boots.
미끄럽다 → 미끄러우니까 (ㅂ-irregular); 장화 = rubber boots
nuance: 갯벌 is the soft, muddy tidal flat that emerges at low tide — a defining feature of Korea's West and South coasts and a beloved hands-on 체험 where families go 조개 캐기 (clam digging). It's a pure native-Korean compound, 개 ('seaside/inlet') + 벌 ('open flat'), joined with a 사이시옷 that adds the ㅅ batchim → 갯벌, which is why the spelling matters. The contrast to nail is 갯벌 vs 해변/모래사장: a 해변 is a firm sandy beach you sunbathe on, while a 갯벌 is wet mud that only exists when the tide is OUT and is tied to 썰물 (low tide) and 밀물 (high tide). The English-speaker pitfall is treating any shoreline as 갯벌 — it specifically means the mud-at-low-tide zone, so don't use it for a regular sandy 해변; also note Korea's 갯벌 are UNESCO-listed, so locals say it with pride, not as 'just mud.'

Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular in 미끄럽다: 'because it's slippery' is 미끄러우니까, not 미끄럽으니까.

usage: Coastal light tower; a very common seaside photo landmark
Ports pair a red and a white one to mark the channel
불빛 = emitted light; what guides ships at night
구경 = casual sightseeing; everyday trip phrasing
examples: 저기 빨간 등대 보여요?
Can you see the red lighthouse over there?
보이다 = to be visible; simple pointing-out question
밤에는 등대 불빛이 멀리까지 보여요.
At night the lighthouse beam is visible from far away.
멀리까지 = all the way far; 까지 = up to/as far as
빨간 등대 쪽으로 산책하면 노을이 진짜 예뻐요.
If you stroll toward the red lighthouse, the sunset is really pretty.
쪽으로 = in the direction of; 노을 = sunset glow
nuance: 등대 (燈臺, 'lamp-platform/tower') is a lighthouse, and on Korean harbor breakwaters you'll famously see a 빨간 등대 (red) and a 하얀/하얀색 등대 (white) marking which side of the channel is which — a beloved backdrop for seaside walks, sunset photos and dates. The hanja 燈 ('lamp') links it to a family of light words, which is exactly the trap: don't confuse 등대 with 등 (a lamp/light) or with the unrelated 등산 (hiking) just because they share 등 sounds. Register is fully neutral and casual, and 등대 also carries a warm figurative sense of a guiding beacon (희망의 등대). The English-speaker pitfall is location particles: for 'meet at the lighthouse' Koreans say 등대 앞에서 / 등대 쪽에서 만나자, because 등대에서 만나자 sounds like meeting literally at its base; and the light it casts is 불빛, not just 빛.

Saying 등대에서 만나자 for a meetup point: more natural is 등대 앞에서 / 등대 쪽에서 만나자, since people gather near it, not at its base.
Using 빛 alone for the beam: the lighthouse's glow is 등대 불빛, the standard collocation.

usage: The whole working waterfront where boats dock
도시 = city; a proud set phrase (Busan is the classic)
a ship comes into the harbor
에 + 들어오다 = to come in toward you
a sashimi place near the harbor
횟집 = raw-fish restaurant; ports mean fresh seafood
examples: 부산은 큰 항구예요.
Busan is a big harbor.
Simple statement; 항구예요 = polite 'is a harbor'
저녁이 되면 항구에 배들이 하나둘 들어와요.
Come evening, ships come into the harbor one by one.
하나둘 = one by one; 들어오다 = come in
항구 앞에서 갓 잡은 생선을 바로 팔아요.
Right by the harbor they sell freshly caught fish on the spot.
갓 잡은 = freshly caught; 바로 = right away/right there
nuance: 항구 (港口, 'port-mouth') is the harbor as a whole — the entire working waterfront of docks, boats and fish markets — strongly tied to Korea's seafood cities like 부산, 속초 and 통영, so it surfaces constantly in 회 (sashimi) trip talk, and 항구 도시 (port city) is a set phrase locals use with pride. The key synonym contrast is 항구 vs 부두: 항구 is the broad harbor area, while 부두 is the specific built pier/wharf where a ship actually ties up — 항구에 도착해서 부두에서 내렸다 shows both. The shared hanja 港 also links it to 공항(空港, airport), the second trap: same character, but 공항 is 'empty-port' = airport, totally different place. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: don't use 항구 for the single pier you board from (that's 부두), and remember a ship 항구에 들어오다/들어가다 (에), since the harbor is the enclosed destination.

Forgetting the verb pairing: a ship 항구에 들어오다 (에 marks the harbor it enters), not 항구를 들어오다.

usage: The built structure where ships tie up and load
여객선 = passenger ship; where island ferries leave
examples: 배는 저 부두에서 타요.
You catch the boat at that pier.
타다 = to board; 에서 marks where you get on
부두를 따라 걸으면서 바다 구경했어요.
We looked at the sea while walking along the pier.
걸으면서 = while walking (ㄷ-irregular 걷다 → 걸으면서)
섬에 가는 배는 저쪽 여객선 부두에서 출발해요.
The boat to the island leaves from that passenger pier over there.
여객선 부두 = ferry terminal; 출발하다 = to depart
nuance: 부두 (埠頭, 'wharf-head') is the concrete pier or wharf where boats physically tie up, load and unload — the built edge of the water, as opposed to 항구 (the whole harbor that surrounds it). You'll reach for it most when catching island ferries (여객선 부두) or strolling a photogenic waterfront, and it collocates with 정박하다 (to moor) and 따라 걷다 (walk along). The synonym line to hold is precisely 부두 vs 항구: 부두 is one specific structure, 항구 is the entire harbor district — slightly more concrete/technical, but still everyday. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't swap 부두 and 항구 freely (English 'dock' blurs them, Korean doesn't), and watch the spelling — 부두, not 부뚜, because 부뚜막 is the ledge of a traditional stove, a completely unrelated word; and to board, you say 부두에서 타다 (에서, the place you board from).

Don't swap 부두 and 항구 freely (English 'dock' blurs them, Korean doesn't), and watch the spelling — 부두, not 부뚜, because 부뚜막 is the ledge of a traditional stove, a completely unrelated word; and to board, you say 부두에서 타다 (에서, the place you board from).

Spelling it 부뚜: the word is 부두; 부뚜(막) is a stove ledge, an entirely different thing.
Saying 부두에 타다 for boarding: the natural form is 부두에서 (배를) 타다, since 에서 marks the place the action departs from.

usage: Wide open grassy or farm land in the countryside
넓다 → 넓은; the most natural pairing
펼쳐지다 = to spread open, used of scenery
examples: 창밖에 넓은 들판이 보여요.
I can see a wide open field outside the window.
창밖 = outside the window; 보이다 = to be seen
가을이 되면 들판이 노랗게 변해요.
When autumn comes, the fields turn yellow.
노랗게 = yellowly (ㅎ-irregular 노랗다); ripening rice
탁 트인 들판에서 자전거 타니까 진짜 시원했어요.
Riding a bike across the wide-open field felt so refreshing.
탁 트이다 = to be wide open; 시원하다 here = liberating
nuance: 들판 is a wide open field or plain — farmland, grassland, the scenery rolling past a countryside train window — and it carries a calm, spacious, rural mood, surfacing especially in 가을 (autumn) when the rice fields turn gold. It's a native compound, 들 ('open country/wild field') + 판 ('flat expanse'). The synonym to separate is 들판 vs 밭: a 밭 is a specific cultivated crop plot (a vegetable field you tend), whereas 들판 is the broad, scenic open expanse — so 밭에서 일하다 (work the field) but 들판이 펼쳐지다 (fields spread out before you). Register is neutral, slightly literary/scenic. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'field' is too broad: a sports field is 운동장, a single crop field is 밭, an academic 'field' is 분야 — reach for 들판 only for the open rural plain, and pair it with 펼쳐지다 or 넓다 rather than translating 'a field of...' literally.

Translating every English 'field' as 들판: a sports field is 운동장 and an area of study is 분야 — 들판 is only the rural open expanse.
Spelling it 들빤 or 들반: the correct form is 들판 (ㄹ batchim + 판).

usage: A small rise, far smaller than a 산 (mountain)
위 = top; 언덕 위 카페 = a hilltop cafe
오르다 = to go up; also 언덕을 올라가다
가파르다 = steep; common for tiring uphill streets
examples: 저기 언덕 위에 집이 있어요.
There's a house up on that hill.
위에 = on top of; 있다 = there is
집까지 가는 길이 언덕이라서 좀 힘들어요.
The way home is uphill, so it's a bit tiring.
언덕이라서 = because it's a slope; 힘들다 = to be tough
봄에는 언덕에 꽃이 잔뜩 펴요.
In spring the hill blooms with tons of flowers.
잔뜩 = a whole lot; 피다 → 펴요 (to bloom)
nuance: 언덕 is a hill or gentle slope — a small rise, far smaller than a 산 (mountain), but enough to make you huff on the walk home — and in Korean cities the hillside neighborhood and the 언덕 위 카페 (hilltop cafe with a view) are a real cultural thing. It's native Korean, and beyond a literal hill it doubles for the tiring incline of a street: 우리 집은 언덕에 있어요 means 'my place is up a slope.' The synonym/scale contrast is the heart of it — don't call a real mountain an 언덕; use 산 for anything you'd actually hike, 언덕 for the small walkable rise (and a steep paved one is 가파른 언덕 or 비탈/비탈길). Register is neutral, often a touch nostalgic. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'hill' and 'mountain' overlap loosely, but Korean draws a firmer line: misusing 언덕 for 설악산 sounds comically small, while calling a neighborhood slope a 산 sounds overdramatic.

Reaching for 산 to describe a steep street: a tiring paved incline is an 언덕 (or 비탈길), not a 산.

usage: An individual mountain peak; a range has several
산 prefixed; a very common combined form
오르다 = to ascend; 정상까지 오르다 is similar
examples: 저기 봉우리가 제일 높아요.
That peak over there is the highest.
제일 높다 = the highest; simple comparison
저 멀리 눈 덮인 봉우리가 보여요.
Off in the distance you can see a snow-covered peak.
눈 덮인 = snow-covered; 보이다 = to be visible
가장 높은 봉우리까지 두 시간쯤 걸려요.
It takes about two hours to reach the highest peak.
가장 높은 = the highest; 걸리다 = to take (time)
nuance: 봉우리 (the 봉 from hanja 峰, 'mountain peak,' plus a native ending) is a single peak or summit, and a ridge or range is understood as several 봉우리 strung together — hikers use it constantly for mountains like 설악산 and 지리산, and the combined 산봉우리 is equally common. The synonym contrast that trips people up is 봉우리 vs 정상: 봉우리 is any one peak among several, while 정상(頂上) is THE very top/highest point you're aiming for — so a mountain can have many 봉우리 but one 정상, and trail talk pairs them (이 봉우리 지나면 정상이에요). Register is neutral, common in hiking and scenery description. The two English-speaker pitfalls: don't equate 봉우리 with 정상 (peak-as-one-of-many vs the single summit), and crucially don't spell it 봉오리 — that's a flower bud, a completely different word, so 산 봉오리 would absurdly mean 'mountain flower-bud.'

mistakes: Treating 봉우리 and 정상 as identical: 봉우리 is one peak among several, while 정상 is the single highest top — a range has many 봉우리 but one 정상.
Spelling it 봉오리: 봉오리 means a flower bud, so the mountain peak must be 봉우리 — a one-vowel slip changes the meaning entirely.
Dropping 산 when context is unclear: in mixed talk 산봉우리 makes 'mountain peak' explicit and avoids ambiguity.

usage: The sandy shore zone; more 'beach' than the open 바다
산책 = stroll; a very common seaside activity
에서 marks where the activity happens
가 (edge) added; 해변가 카페 = a beachfront cafe
examples: 여름에 강릉 해변에 갔어요.
In summer I went to Gangneung beach.
강릉 = Gangneung; 에 가다 = go to (a place)
해변을 따라 걸으니까 노을이 너무 예뻤어요.
Walking along the beach, the sunset was so pretty.
따라 = along; 노을 = sunset glow
해변에 사람이 별로 없어서 조용했어요.
There weren't many people on the beach, so it was quiet.
별로 + 없다 = not many; 조용하다 = to be quiet
nuance: 해변 (海邊, 'sea-edge') is specifically the sandy beach/shore strip, while 바다 is the sea itself — the distinction is concrete: you lay your towel and stroll on the 해변, but you swim in the 바다, so 해변에서 수영하다 sounds slightly off (you're on the sand, not in the water). East-coast spots like 강릉 and 속초 are the go-to 해변, and it collocates with 산책 (stroll) and 노을 (sunset). The other near-synonym is 해수욕장(海水浴場, 'sea-water-bathing place'): 해변 is the natural shore generally, whereas 해수욕장 is a designated, facility-equipped swimming beach (lifeguards, showers, the official summer-open kind) — overlapping but not identical. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 바다/해변 split: English 'go to the beach' covers both lying out and swimming, but in Korean you 해변에 가다 to be on the shore and 바다에 들어가다 to get in the water.
